title: Mechanostimulation of Multicellular Organisms Through a High-Throughput Microfluidic Compression System
protocol: Clean the silicon wafer with acetone.
Clean the silicon wafer with isopropyl alcohol.
Place the silicon wafer on a 250 °C hot plate for 30 min.
Coat the silicon wafer with hexamethyldisilazane (HDMS) in a vapor prime oven at 150 °C and 2 Torr for 5 min.
Place a bottle of SU-8 2100 photoresist in a 60 °C oven for 15 min.
Pour 1 mL of heated photoresist on the silicon wafer for each inch until it covers most of the surface.
Place the photoresist-coated silicon wafer on a spin coater.
Apply pre-spin at 250 rpm for 30 s with 100 rpm/s acceleration.
Apply pre-spin at 350 rpm for another 30 s with 100 rpm/s acceleration.
Remove excess photoresist from the edges of the wafer using a cleanroom swab.
Spin the wafer first at 500 rpm for 15 s with 100 rpm/s acceleration.
Spin the wafer at 1450 rpm for 30 s with 300 rpm/s acceleration.
Remove edge bead from the wafer with a cleanroom swab.
Place the silicon wafer on a 50 °C hot plate.
Spray acetone onto the silicon wafer to remove imperfections and promote uniform coating.
Ramp up the temperature of the hot plate to 95 °C at a rate of 2°C/min.
Soft bake the silicon wafer at 95 °C for 50 min.
Slowly cool down the hot plate to room temperature at a rate of 2°C/min.
Place the silicon wafer on a mask aligner.
Place the photomask on top of the silicon wafer.
Expose the silicon wafer to 350 mJ/cm² UV light through the photomask using the contact mask aligner.
Apply post-exposure bake at 50 °C for 5 min.
Continue baking at 65 °C for an additional 5 min.
Finally, bake at 80 °C for another 20 min.
Slowly cool down the silicon wafer to room temperature at a rate of 2°C/min.
Place a magnetic stirrer in a beaker with a slightly smaller diameter than the silicon wafer.
Turn the silicon wafer upside-down and place it on top of the beaker.
Submerge the silicon wafer in a fresh developer solution for 30 min with stirring.
Transfer the silicon wafer into an ultrasonic bath filled with a fresh developer solution.
Sonicate the silicon wafer at 40 kHz for 1 hour.
Thoroughly wash the silicon wafer with an IPA solution.
Place the silicon wafer mold in a desiccator with 10 drops of Trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl)silane.
Connect the desiccator to a vacuum pump at approximately 200 Torr for 30 min.
Turn off the desiccator valve and disconnect the vacuum pump overnight for PFOCTS coating.
Mix the PDMS base with the curing agent at a 10:1 ratio.
Place the mixture into a centrifuge (500 x g for 5 min) to degas.
Pour the degassed PDMS solution onto the silicon wafer mold.
Degas again to remove air bubbles trapped on the mold surface.
Cure the PDMS in a 60 °C oven for 1 h and 50 min.
Cut the borders of the cured PDMS region corresponding to the microfluidic chip geometry.
Peel the PDMS part and place it upside-down on a cutting mat.
Use a razor to cut the PDMS part into its final shape.
Punch inlet and outlet holes on PDMS using a biopsy punch or needle with a blunt tip.
For the embryo inlet hole, use a 4 mm diameter punch.
Use a 1.3 mm diameter punch for embryo outlet holes.
Use a 2 mm punch for the gas inlet hole.
Remove any particulate on the PDMS patterned surface with scotch tape.
Clean a 24 mm x 60 mm rectangular glass slide first with acetone and then with IPA.
Dry the glass surface with an air gun connected to a filtered air source.
Apply a dehydration bake to the glass slide by placing it on a 250 °C hot plate for 2 h.
Cover the glass slide with a beaker during baking to prevent surface contamination.
Treat PDMS and dehydrated glass slide with oxygen plasma at 18 W for 30 s in a plasma cleaner.
Place PDMS, patterned side up, on the dehydrated glass slide to seal microchannels via covalent bonding.
Gently push PDMS against the glass slide with tweezers to ensure full conformational contact.
Store completed microfluidic chip at room temperature overnight for bonding to reach final strength.
Allow Oregon-R adult flies to lay eggs on apple juice agar plates (1.5% agar, 25% apple juice, 2.5% sucrose).
Collect plates containing embryos at the desired developmental time after egg laying.
Collect plates at 140 min to prepare and sort for embryos at the cellularization stage.
Flood the agar with embryo egg wash and gently agitate the embryos with a paintbrush.
Transfer the embryos to a 50% bleach solution for 90 seconds, stirring occasionally.
Strain the embryos through a tissue sieve and thoroughly wash away the bleach solution with water.
Transfer the embryos to a 90 mm glass Petri dish with enough embryo egg wash to cover them fully.
Examine the embryos with transillumination on a dissecting microscope.
Select embryos of the desired development stage for loading into the microfluidic device.
Prime all seven embryo microchannels by filling them with 0.4 μm filtered IPA through the main embryo inlet port.
Replace the IPA with 0.4 μm filtered deionized (DI) water.
Replace the DI water with embryo egg wash solution.
Collect approximately 100 preselected embryos from the glass Petri dish using a glass pipette.
Pipette the embryos into the embryo inlet port.
Apply an approximately 3 PSI negative pressure to the gas inlet using a portable vacuum pump to open up the embryo microchannels.
Tilt the microfluidic chip downward to align and settle embryos into embryo microchannels.
If clogging occurs at embryo microchannel inlets, tilt the chip upward then downward again to clear it.
Introduce up to 300 embryos into the embryo microchannels based on required throughput.
Remove vacuum once embryo loading is completed to immobilize the embryos.
Tilt the microfluidic chip back to the horizontal position.
Connect a portable positive pressure source with a gauge to the gas inlet and apply 3 PSI compression.
Check the pressure gauge continuously to ensure consistent compression level.
If conducting live imaging, place the microfluidic chip on a microscope stage glass slide holder connected to the pressure source.
Once the experiment is completed, apply vacuum to the gas inlet to free the embryos for collection.
Tilt the microfluidic chip upward to move embryos toward the embryo introduction port.
Collect embryos from the microfluidic chip using a glass pipette.
